Description of Wastewater and Biosolids Treatment and Controls The treatment system at the Facility includes two plants (Plant 1 and Plant 2). The Discharger completed construction of Facility upgrades during the last permit term. With improvements made at Plant 1 and Plant 2, the majority of Plant 1 is decommissioned, and Plant 2 is the central treatment facility. The upgraded Facility is operational as of June 2023 and consists of the following treatment system: Headworks: The Facility headworks are located at Plant 1 and 2. chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: A pilot-scale plexiglas Carrousel oxidation ditch was constructed, in which three semicircular channels were connected to four 1.15-m long straight channels. The ditch was 0.35-m wide and 0.5-m deep with a total working volume of 1.4 m 3 . Air was introduced from four 1-m long microporous aerator pipes located at the base of the second and third channels. The sketch of the reactor can be found in the supplementary information (SI). Experimental activated sludge was seeded from a steady-running SBR process in a municipal WWTP. The COD and NH 4 + -N concentration of synthetic wastewater were controlled at 250 mg L −1 and 50 mg L −1 , and pH was approximately 7.8 without adjustment. The liquor temperature was maintained at 22 ± 2 °C with a heating rod. Before getting into the inlet of the first channel, the influent and returned sludge were firstly pumped into a 50-L bioselector with continuous blending to avoid sludge bulking problem. The variations of HRT and SRT were achieved by altering the daily influent and sludge discharge rate.

chunks.citation: Ma, Y et al. (2009). Achieving nitrogen removal via nitrite in a pilot-scale continuous pre-denitrification plant. nan.
chunks.text:
The traditional biological nitrogen removal processes utilized in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) involve the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 þ ) to nitrate (NO 3 À ) (nitrification) followed by nitrate reduction with an organic carbon source to nitrogen gas (N 2 ) (denitrification). Both nitrification and denitrification possess nitrite (NO 2 À ) as an intermediate. Hence, if

nitrification is stopped at nitrite, denitritation from nitrite to nitrogen gas can be achieved (Verstraete et al., 1977) . Nitrogen removal via nitrite yields 25% reduction in oxygen demand for nitrification and 40% reduction in chemical oxygen demand (COD) requirement for denitrification (Pollice et al., 2002; Turk and Mavinic, 1987) . The reduction in COD requirement would be particularly advantageous for WWTPs treating wastewater with a low COD to nitrogen ratio.

chunks.text: AOPs have been identified as an effective means to treat these complex effluents due to their ability to produce powerful oxidizing agents such as hydroxyl radicals ( • OH) insitu [3] . The strength and non-selectivity of • OH as an oxidizing agent enables the complete mineralization of a wide range of organic compounds at first order rates in the magnitude of 10 6 to 10 9 M − 1 s − 1 [4] . Although many approaches are available to produce • OH for use in water and wastewater treatment applications, AOPs generally consist of combinations of various chemical reagents (ozone and hydrogen peroxide) and external energy sources (UV-VIS radiation). While the non-selectivity of • OH as an oxidant makes AOPs viable in numerous applications, their potential to be utilized more prevalently is limited by the high cost of the aforementioned reagents [5] . As a result, low-cost alternatives or innovations to traditional AOPs are required to allow these treatment processes to become available for industrial source control in small and decentralized applications while also improving the efficiency of current applications.

chunks.text: With the rapid development of industrialization and modernization, the global production of wastewater has grown significantly. As a byproduct of wastewater treatment, the production of sludge has increased substantially accordingly, leading to a dramatic increase in energy consumption (E c ) and disposal costs. Municipal sludge poses a series of challenges for further disposal because of high moisture content (M c ). Therefore, sludge dewatering is the primary step for achieving sludge reduction, harmless treatment, and resource recovery [5, 41] . Mechanical press filtration (MPF) is one of the most commonly used for sludge dewatering. This method can reduce M c of sludge to 60-80 %, which cannot meet the current and future lower M c requirements [30] . MPF can only remove the relatively easy-to-remove free water and causes clogging and deformation of the micro-pore and voids in sludge cake [31] . Therefore, to address this issue, equipment optimization and pressure parameters optimization have been the significant research topics, such as using ultra-high MPF. Iritani et al. [16] studied dewatering under ultrasonic pretreatment at 50 MPa, reducing M c of sludge to 38 %.

Drying rates ranged between 1 and 40 g/min/m 2 , leading to drying times comprised between 100 and 300 min. The drying kinetics increased as temperature was higher, and pellet diameter and relative humidity were lower. Temperature had the greatest influence on the drying kinetics (in both the constant and falling rate periods), followed by the effect of pellet diameter. The drying kinetics were affected in a moderate way by the relative humidity in the constant rate period and part of the falling rate period. The air velocity had a slight effect of drying kinetics during the constant rate period, but this becomes insignificant during the falling rate period. The effective diffusivities increased from 7.81 Â 10 À8 to 1.97 Â 10 À7 m 2 /s by increasing the temperature from 40 to 80 C, leading to an activation energy of 23 kJ/mol. These values are typical from those found for wastewater sludge. The sludge exhibited a critical moisture content varying between 2.4 and 3.2 g/g db during drying without a clear trend as a function of the operating conditions and suggested that sludge was composed of considerably more bound moisture than unbound.

chunks.text: BHSD is a secondary municipal water resource recovery facility (WRRF) with an annual average flowrate of 1170 m 3 ⋅d − 1 (0.31 mgd) and design (peak) flowrate of 4540 m 3 ⋅d − 1 (1.2 mgd). It receives primarily municipal wastewater with heavier flows from restaurants associated with tourism during the summer months. Discharge in the summer months during peak tourism season average 1325 m 3 ⋅d − 1 (0.35 mgd), and during the winter off-season average 1098 m 3 ⋅d − 1 (0.29 mgd). The WRRF operates with two sequencing batch reactor (SBR) tanks providing sedimentation and biological treatment following centrifugation for grit removal. Chlorine disinfection is practiced between mid-May to the end of September, before discharge to Boothbay Harbor. A centrifuge is used for sludge dewatering prior to biosolids composting and land application, both of which occur off-site.

Calafell WWTP was built on 1994 to treat the wastewaters of the municipalities of Calafell and Bellveí and designed for 70,000 population equivalent with a maximum flow of 12,000 m 3 /day. After a primary treatment, wastewater is treated in two activated sludge reactors with extended aeration including nitrogen removal, followed by the secondary settler. From these units, the treated wastewater is directly discharged to the submarine sewage. Some differences are observed in the operation of the plant between winter and summer seasons due to fluctuations on the population and changes on the influent composition. A coagulation-flocculation treatment, only operated during summer, receives the wastewater after the screening step.

chunks.text: Based on a survey on pre-treatment measures for 17 full-scale AeMBRs, the following information deserves special attention (Itokawa et al., 2008) : 1) grit chamber, coarse and fine screenings are mostly essential for MBR operation to removal grits, large suspended particles and long fibers, with fine screening (3 mm for FS membrane and 0.5-1 mm for HF membrane) installed universally; and 2) using the "by pass sieving" method, which recycles part of the suspended sludge through a sieve, achieves the further removal of unfavorable substances accumulated in the bioreactor. These means can be extended to AnMBRs minimizing the presence of undesirable substances into the bioreactor while with adequate consideration of keeping strict anaerobic environment. A recent novel concept, referred to as wastewater pre-concentration (Ansari et al., 2016) , is still under investigation, but has shown great potential to enhance bioresource recovery and energy generation efficiency (Guven et al., 2019) , accompanied by a low volumetric flow rate and process footprint (Alvarado et al., 2020) .
